title: The Library Club's Big Idea
summary: A small after-school library club worries that nobody wants to join, until a reading challenge and a book-recommendation wall make the library popular with classmates.
poll: A small group with a good idea can get a whole school excited about something.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Sara, Omar, and Lina run a club. It is a library club. They meet on Tuesdays.

But just three kids come. No one else joins. Sara feels sad.

The three friends sit and think. They want a new idea. They want more kids to come.

First, they make a game. It is a book game. Kids read mystery books for it. Each book gets a sticker.

Next, they make a wall. It is by the door. Kids pin notes on it. The notes tell about good books. Other kids read the notes. Then they pick a new book.

Sara paints big signs. Omar and Lina help her. They show the signs to the whole school. Many kids like the new ideas.

Soon, more kids come to the club. The library gets busy. It is full of fun. The teacher is glad. One small idea made a big change.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Sara, Omar, and Lina run a small club. It is a library club. They meet every Tuesday.

But only three kids come. No one else joins them. Sara feels sad.

One day, the friends sit and think. They want a new idea. They want more kids to come.

First, they make a fun game. It is about mystery books. Kids who read a book get a sticker.

Next, they build a wall by the door. Kids pin notes on the wall. The notes tell about good books. Other kids read the notes and pick a new book.

Sara paints big, bright signs. Omar and Lina help her. They show the signs to the school. Many kids like the new ideas.

Soon, more kids start to come. The library feels busy on Tuesday. The teacher is proud of the friends. One small idea made a big change.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Sara, Omar, and Lina run a small library club. The club meets every Tuesday after class. But only the three of them show up. Sara feels worried about this.

One afternoon, the three friends sit in the library. They want to find a new idea. They want more kids to join the club.

Their first idea is a reading game. It is called Mystery Month. A kid who reads a mystery book earns a sticker. Enough stickers earn a small prize.

Their second idea is a book wall. It is a wall by the library door. Kids pin short notes about books they liked. Other kids look at the wall. Then they pick a new book to read.

Sara paints bright signs about both ideas. Omar and Lina help her show the signs to the whole school. Many kids seem glad about the new plans.

Over the next few weeks, more kids start to come every Tuesday. The library feels busy, not quiet. Their teacher says she is proud, because one small idea changed their little club.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Sara, Omar, and Lina run a small library club. It meets every Tuesday after class. Yet week after week, only the three of them show up. Sara feels more worried about this.

One quiet afternoon, the friends sit among the bookshelves. They want to find a fresh idea. They hope more kids will join the club.

Their first idea is a reading game they call Mystery Month. A kid who finishes a mystery book earns a sticker on a chart. Enough stickers earn a small prize.

Their second idea is a book wall. It is a wall right by the library door. Kids pin short notes about books they liked. Other kids look at the wall and pick a new book to try.

Sara paints several bright signs about both ideas. Omar and Lina help her carry the signs to the school. Many kids seem glad once they hear the new plans.

Over the next few weeks, more kids start to come every Tuesday. The once-quiet library feels busy and full of fun. Their teacher tells them how proud she is, because one small idea changed their tiny club.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday, Sara, Omar, and Lina unlock the library door. They set out chairs for the after-school club. For weeks, almost no one else shows up. Sara worries the club might end if it cannot gain more members soon.

One afternoon, the friends sit among the bookshelves. They hope to think of something new. Just asking kids to join is not enough. They need an idea that sparks real curiosity and feels exciting.

Their first idea is a reading challenge called Mystery Month. Any student who finishes a mystery book earns a sticker. The sticker goes on a big chart by the door. Enough stickers earn a small prize.

Their second idea is a book wall. It is a wall beside the library door. Students pin short notes to recommend books they enjoyed. Classmates who feel unsure what to read can look at the wall. They quickly find something new to try.

Sara paints several bright signs to spread the word. Omar and Lina help her share both ideas with the school. Many students who never visited the library seem suddenly curious.

Over the next few weeks, more kids keep showing up. The once-quiet library feels busy every Tuesday. Their teacher praises the three friends warmly. She says one small idea turned a forgotten club into a popular one.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday, Sara, Omar, and Lina unlock the library door and set out chairs for the after-school club, hoping this week might finally be different. For weeks, almost no one else shows up. Sara worries the club might end if it cannot gain more members soon.

One afternoon, the three friends sit together among the bookshelves, hoping to think of something new that might finally spark their classmates' interest. Simply asking kids to join is not enough. The club needs an idea that feels exciting instead of ordinary and repeated.

Their first idea becomes a reading challenge they decide to call Mystery Month. Any student who finishes an entire mystery book earns a sticker on a big chart near the door, and enough stickers earn a small prize, such as a bookmark or a free snack.

Their second idea, a book wall, grows popular within just a few days. It is a wall beside the library door where students pin short notes to recommend books they truly enjoyed reading. Classmates who feel unsure what to read next can glance at the crowded wall and quickly find something worth trying.

Sara carefully paints several bright signs to spread the word throughout the whole school. Omar and Lina help her share both new ideas with their classmates at a school meeting. Many students who had rarely visited the library before now seem suddenly curious about the growing club.

Over the next few weeks, more and more kids keep showing up, until the once-quiet library feels busy and lively every single Tuesday. Their teacher praises the three friends warmly, pointing out that one thoughtful idea, built from nothing but curiosity, turned a nearly forgotten club into a popular one.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday, Sara, Omar, and Lina unlock the library door and set out chairs for the after-school club, each time hoping this particular week might turn out differently. For weeks on end, almost no one else shows up. Sara worries that the club might be canceled if the group cannot attract more members soon enough.

One afternoon, the three friends sit together among the bookshelves. They are determined to think of something that might spark their classmates' curiosity about reading. Simply announcing another meeting will not be enough on its own. What the club truly needs is an idea that feels genuinely exciting.

Their first idea becomes a themed reading challenge they decide to call Mystery Month. Any student who finishes an entire mystery book earns a sticker on a big chart near the door, and collecting enough stickers earns a small prize, such as a bookmark or a snack.

Their second idea, which they call a book wall, grows almost as popular within just a few days. It is a wall beside the library door where students pin short notes to recommend books they genuinely enjoyed reading. Classmates who feel unsure what to read next can glance at the crowded wall and quickly find something worth trying.

Sara carefully paints several bright signs to spread the word throughout the school. Omar and Lina help her present both ideas to their classmates at a school meeting. Many students who had rarely visited the library before now seem suddenly curious about Mystery Month and the growing book wall.

Over the following weeks, attendance at the club grows steadily, until the once-quiet library feels lively and busy every single Tuesday. Their teacher praises the three friends warmly, pointing out that one thoughtful idea, built from nothing more than curiosity, managed to turn a nearly forgotten club into one of the most popular clubs at school.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday afternoon, three friends named Sara, Omar, and Lina unlock the library door and arrange chairs for the after-school club. Each week they hope this Tuesday might turn out differently than the ones before it. Yet almost no one else bothers to show up, and attendance never climbs above the three organizers themselves, even after they post friendly reminders near the cafeteria and the gym.

Sara worries that the principal might eventually cancel the struggling club unless the group can attract more members fairly soon. One quiet afternoon, the friends sit together among the crowded bookshelves. They are determined to brainstorm something that might spark their classmates' genuine curiosity about reading, instead of making it feel like an obligation, rather than repeating the same quiet announcements that nobody seems to notice.

Their first idea develops into a themed reading challenge they enthusiastically decide to call Mystery Month. Any student who completes a mystery novel earns a colorful sticker on a chart near the door. Collecting enough stickers earns a small prize, such as a bookmark, a modest incentive that students enjoy.

Their second idea, which they label a book wall, grows nearly as popular within just a few days. It is a wall beside the library entrance where students pin short notes recommending books they genuinely enjoyed, and within a week the wall is nearly covered in colorful notes.

To spread the word, Sara carefully paints several bright, eye-catching signs. Omar and Lina help her present both initiatives confidently during a school meeting. Many students who had rarely visited the library before now seem suddenly curious about Mystery Month and the growing book wall.

Over the following weeks, attendance at the club grows steadily, until the once-quiet library feels genuinely lively every single Tuesday. Their teacher praises the three friends warmly, noting that one thoughtful idea, built from curiosity and a bit of creativity, transformed a nearly forgotten club into one of the most popular activities at school.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday afternoon, three determined friends named Sara, Omar, and Lina unlocked the library door and arranged chairs for their after-school club, each week hoping this particular Tuesday might finally turn out differently from the discouraging ones that had preceded it, though attendance never climbed above the three organizers themselves, even after they posted friendly reminders near the cafeteria and the gym entrance each week.

Sara worried, with increasing seriousness, that the principal might eventually decide to cancel the struggling club unless the group managed to attract a meaningful number of additional members before the term ended, so one quiet afternoon the three friends sat together among the crowded bookshelves, determined to brainstorm something sufficiently imaginative to spark their classmates' curiosity about reading for pleasure rather than obligation.

Their first idea developed into a themed reading challenge they enthusiastically named Mystery Month, in which any student who completed an entire mystery novel earned a colorful sticker on a chart near the library door, and accumulating enough stickers eventually earned a small prize, such as a bookmark or a free snack, a modest incentive that nevertheless proved surprisingly motivating given how little it cost the small club to provide.

Their second idea, which they eventually labeled a book wall, grew nearly as popular within only a few days of being introduced to the wider student body, since it was simply a wall positioned beside the library entrance where students pinned short, handwritten notes recommending books they had genuinely enjoyed, so that classmates feeling uncertain about what to read next could glance at the increasingly crowded wall and quickly discover something worth trying.

To spread the word throughout the school, Sara carefully painted several bright, eye-catching signs, while Omar and Lina helped her present both initiatives confidently during a school-wide gathering, and many students who had rarely, if ever, visited the library voluntarily now seemed suddenly curious about Mystery Month and the increasingly popular book wall taking shape near the entrance.

Over the following weeks, attendance grew steadily and consistently, until the once-quiet library felt genuinely lively every single Tuesday afternoon without exception, and their teacher praised the three friends warmly during a staff meeting, specifically noting that one thoughtful initiative, built from nothing more than curiosity and a modest amount of creativity, had managed to transform a nearly forgotten club into one of the most popular activities offered anywhere in the entire school.

versions.title: The Library Club's Big Idea
versions.text:
Every Tuesday afternoon, three determined friends named Sara, Omar, and Lina unlocked the library door and arranged chairs for their after-school club, each week hoping, perhaps a little unrealistically, that this particular Tuesday might finally turn out differently from the discouraging ones that had repeatedly preceded it, even though attendance never climbed above the three organizers themselves, who privately wondered whether their classmates even remembered that the small, struggling club continued to exist at all.

Sara worried, with increasing seriousness, that the principal might eventually decide to cancel the club altogether unless the group managed to attract a genuinely meaningful number of additional members before the academic term drew to a close, so one quiet afternoon the three friends sat together among the crowded bookshelves, determined to brainstorm something sufficiently imaginative to spark their classmates' authentic curiosity about reading for pleasure rather than mere academic obligation.

Their first idea developed into a themed reading challenge they enthusiastically named Mystery Month, in which any student who completed an entire mystery novel earned a colorful sticker on a chart displayed prominently near the library door, and accumulating enough stickers eventually earned a modest prize, such as a bookmark or a free snack during lunchtime, an incentive that nevertheless proved surprisingly motivating given how little it actually cost the club to provide.

Their second idea, which they eventually labeled a book wall, grew nearly as popular within only a few days of being introduced to the wider student body, since it was simply a wall positioned directly beside the library entrance where students pinned short, handwritten notes recommending books they had genuinely enjoyed, so that classmates feeling uncertain about what to read next could glance at the increasingly crowded wall and quickly discover something worth trying without consulting anyone else at all.

To spread the word throughout the entire school, Sara carefully painted several bright, eye-catching signs, while Omar and Lina helped her present both initiatives confidently during a school-wide gathering, and many students who had rarely, if ever, visited the library voluntarily before now seemed suddenly and visibly curious about Mystery Month and the increasingly popular book wall gradually taking shape near the entrance.

Over the following weeks, attendance grew steadily and consistently, until the once-quiet library felt genuinely lively and crowded every single Tuesday afternoon without a single exception, and their teacher praised the three friends warmly during a staff meeting, specifically noting that one thoughtful initiative, built from nothing more than curiosity and a modest amount of creativity, had managed to transform a nearly forgotten club into one of the most popular after-school activities offered anywhere in the entire school.

keyWords.definition: a group of people who meet because they like the same thing
keyWords.example: My brother joined a soccer club at his school.

keyWords.definition: a new thought or plan in your mind
keyWords.example: I had an idea for a fun game we could play at recess.

keyWords.definition: a flat, upright side of a room or building
keyWords.example: We hung a big calendar on the wall near the door.

keyWords.definition: to become part of a group
keyWords.example: Three new kids want to join our art club this week.

keyWords.definition: a room or building full of books that people can read or borrow
keyWords.example: I borrow two new books from the library every week.

questions.stem: What is this story mostly about?
options: Three friends who plant a garden at school
Three friends who find a new way to get kids to join their library club
A teacher who closes the school library
A class that goes on a field trip to another school
questions.why: The story tells how Sara, Omar, and Lina get more kids to join their club with a reading challenge and a book wall.

wrong.A: The story is not about a garden.
wrong.C: The library does not close in the story. It gets busier.
wrong.D: There is no field trip in the story.

questions.stem: Why does Sara feel sad at the start of the story?
options: Only three kids come to the library club
She lost her favorite book
She did not get a sticker
Her friends moved to a new school
questions.why: The story says only three kids come to the club, and Sara feels sad about it.

wrong.B: The story does not say Sara lost a book.
wrong.C: Stickers come later, after the new idea.
wrong.D: Her friends do not move away.

questions.stem: What happens right after the three friends decide to find a new idea?
options: They close the library club
They plan Mystery Month and the book wall
They ask the teacher to pick new kids
They stop meeting on Tuesdays
questions.why: After deciding to find a new idea, the friends plan the reading challenge and the book wall.

wrong.C: The teacher does not pick kids for them.
wrong.D: They keep meeting on Tuesdays.

questions.stem: In the story, a book wall is —
options: a wall made of real books stacked up
a wall that keeps kids out of the library
a wall with notes that tell about good books
a wall where kids draw pictures of animals
questions.why: The story says kids write notes about books they like and pin them on the wall for others to read.

wrong.B: The wall does not keep kids out.
wrong.D: The notes are about books, not animal pictures.

questions.stem: Why do kids like the book wall?
options: It gives them free snacks every day
It helps them pick a new book to read
It lets them skip their homework
It tells them when school starts
questions.why: The notes on the wall help kids who are not sure what to read find a new book they might like.

wrong.A: Snacks are only part of the reading challenge prize, not the wall.
wrong.C: The story does not say kids skip homework.
wrong.D: The wall is about books, not school times.

questions.stem: What can you tell about Sara, Omar, and Lina from the story?
options: They do not care about their club
They want the club to stay small
They want to stop reading books
They work together to solve a problem
questions.why: The three friends think together, make signs together, and share both new ideas, showing they work as a team.

wrong.B: They want more kids to join, not fewer.
wrong.C: They love reading; that is why the club exists.

questions.stem: Why does the author tell us that the library becomes busy and fun at the end?
options: To show that the new ideas worked well
To show that the library closed early
To show that the teacher was angry
To show that the signs were lost
questions.why: The busy, fun library at the end shows readers that Mystery Month and the book wall were a success.

wrong.C: The teacher is proud, not angry.
wrong.D: The signs are shown at the school meeting, not lost.

questions.stem: How are the reading challenge and the book wall alike?
options: They both happen outside the school
They both help make the library club more popular
They both are about sports, not books
They both happen only one time
questions.why: Both ideas get kids interested in reading and bring more students to the club.

wrong.C: Both are about books.
wrong.D: The book wall keeps growing, and Mystery Month lasts for weeks.

LOW.prompt: Would you like to join the library club in the story? Explain why or why not, using at least two facts from the story.
checklist: I clearly said what I think.
I used at least two facts from the story.
I wrote complete sentences with capital letters and periods.
LOW.modelAnswer: I would like to join the library club in the story. I would want to try Mystery Month, because reading mystery books and getting stickers sounds fun. I would also like the book wall, because I do not always know what book to read next. The notes from other kids would help me pick a good one.

keyWords.definition: a person who belongs to a group or club
keyWords.example: Every member of the chess club gets a name tag.

keyWords.definition: to tell someone that something is good and worth trying
keyWords.example: My cousin recommended a funny movie for family night.

keyWords.definition: a task or activity that tests what someone can do
keyWords.example: The teacher gave the class a challenge to read five books by June.

keyWords.definition: liked or enjoyed by many people
keyWords.example: The new park became popular with kids in the neighborhood.

keyWords.definition: a strong wish to learn or know more about something
keyWords.example: Her curiosity about space led her to read many science books.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the story?
options: Three students use creative ideas to grow their library club and make it popular.
A librarian decides to remove all the mystery books from the shelves.
A school cancels every after-school club because of low attendance.
A student wins a prize for reading the most books in the whole school.
questions.why: The story follows Sara, Omar, and Lina as they create Mystery Month and the book wall to grow their small club.

wrong.B: The story is about adding a mystery reading challenge, not removing books.
wrong.C: Only the library club is at risk, and it is not canceled.
wrong.D: The story does not focus on one winner; it focuses on the whole club growing.

questions.stem: Why are Sara, Omar, and Lina worried at the beginning of the story?
options: They cannot find enough mystery books
Attendance at their club never grows past the three of them
The library closes every Tuesday
Their teacher wants to cancel the book wall
questions.why: The story says attendance never climbs above the three organizers, and Sara worries the club might be canceled.

wrong.A: Finding books is not mentioned as a problem.
wrong.C: The library is open on Tuesdays; that is when the club meets.
wrong.D: The book wall has not been created yet at this point in the story.

questions.stem: What reward can a student earn by collecting enough stickers in Mystery Month?
options: A free trip to another school
A brand-new library card for every student
A small prize, such as a bookmark
A chance to skip a reading quiz
questions.why: The story says collecting enough stickers earns a small prize, such as a bookmark or a small treat.

wrong.A: There is no trip mentioned in the story.
wrong.B: Library cards are not part of the challenge.
wrong.D: A reading quiz is not mentioned in the story.

questions.stem: Why do more students become curious about the library after the school meeting?
options: The signs and announcement introduce exciting new ideas
The principal orders every student to join
The library offers free lunch to visitors
The teacher gives everyone a mystery novel
questions.why: Sara's signs and the friends' presentation at the school meeting make classmates curious about Mystery Month and the book wall.

wrong.B: No one is ordered to join; students choose to come.
wrong.C: Free lunch is not mentioned in the story.
wrong.D: The teacher does not hand out novels in the story.

questions.stem: In the story, when students recommend a book, they —
options: tell the librarian to remove the book from the shelf
tell other students that a book is worth trying
ask a teacher to read the book out loud
take the book home without returning it
questions.why: Students write notes on the book wall recommending books they enjoyed, which means telling others the books are worth trying.

wrong.A: Recommending a book is not about removing it.
wrong.C: The story does not mention reading aloud.
wrong.D: The story does not discuss taking books home.

questions.stem: Why might a student who feels unsure about what to read find the book wall helpful?
options: It lists every rule of the library
It shows notes from classmates about books they liked
It shows a map of where every book is kept
It tells students which books are too hard to read
questions.why: The book wall is full of short notes recommending books, which helps an unsure reader choose something new.

wrong.A: The wall is about recommendations, not library rules.
wrong.C: The story does not mention a map.
wrong.D: The wall highlights books students enjoyed, not books that are too hard.

questions.stem: How does the author organize the events in the story?
options: By comparing two different schools in every paragraph
By describing the problem, the new ideas, and then the result of those ideas
By listing steps to build library shelves
By telling the story backward, starting with the ending
questions.why: The story first shows the low attendance problem, then the two new ideas, and finally how those ideas made the club popular.

wrong.A: Only one school appears in the story.
wrong.C: The story is not about building shelves.
wrong.D: The story moves forward in time, not backward.

questions.stem: How are Mystery Month and the book wall similar as club ideas?
options: Both ideas take place far away from the school
Both ideas give students a reason to be curious about reading
Both ideas require students to write a long essay
Both ideas happen only one single time
questions.why: Mystery Month and the book wall both spark students' curiosity and give them new reasons to read.

wrong.A: Both happen right at the school, near the library.
wrong.C: Neither idea requires an essay.
wrong.D: The book wall keeps growing, and Mystery Month runs for a month.

MID.prompt: Explain how Sara, Omar, and Lina solve the club's problem. Use at least two details from the story.
checklist: I explained the club's problem and how it was solved.
I used at least two details from the story.
I organized my ideas in a clear order.
MID.modelAnswer: At the start of the story, Sara, Omar, and Lina worry because only the three of them ever come to the library club. To fix this, they create Mystery Month, a reading challenge where students earn stickers and small prizes for reading mystery books. They also create a book wall, where students recommend books to each other with short notes. After the friends share both ideas at the school meeting, more students grow curious and start showing up every Tuesday, which saves the club.

keyWords.definition: a new plan or action taken to solve a problem or improve something
keyWords.example: The student council launched an initiative to clean up the playground.

keyWords.definition: showing strong excitement or interest in something
keyWords.example: The new coach was enthusiastic about starting the swim team.

keyWords.definition: something that encourages a person to do a particular thing
keyWords.example: Extra recess time was a strong incentive for the class to finish early.

keyWords.definition: to change something completely, often making it much better
keyWords.example: New paint and plants transformed the dull courtyard into a cheerful space.

keyWords.definition: something a person feels required or expected to do
keyWords.example: He finished his project early instead of leaving it as a last-minute obligation.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the story?
options: A small, struggling club is transformed when its members design initiatives that make reading feel genuinely exciting.
A principal forces every student to attend an after-school club against their will.
A library closes permanently because too few students show any interest in reading.
Three students compete against each other to see who can read the most books.
questions.why: The story centers on how Sara, Omar, and Lina's initiatives, Mystery Month and the book wall, turn a nearly forgotten club into a popular one.

wrong.B: No student is forced to attend; interest grows naturally.
wrong.C: The library does not close; it becomes busier.
wrong.D: The three friends cooperate rather than compete with one another.

questions.stem: Why does Sara worry that the principal might cancel the club?
options: The library was damaged by a bad storm last spring
The school decided to remove all mystery novels from the shelves
Attendance never grows beyond the three organizers themselves
Omar and Lina want to quit the reading club entirely
questions.why: The story explains that attendance never climbs above the three friends, which makes Sara fear the club could be canceled.

wrong.A: No storm or damage is mentioned.
wrong.B: Mystery novels are added to the challenge, not removed.
wrong.D: Omar and Lina help build the new initiatives rather than quitting.

questions.stem: What incentive motivates students to finish mystery novels during Mystery Month?
options: A guaranteed spot on the student council
A sticker and the chance to earn a small prize
A private meeting with the principal
A certificate signed by every teacher in the school
questions.why: The story states that finishing a mystery novel earns a sticker, and enough stickers earn a small prize, like a bookmark or snack.

wrong.A: Student council membership is never mentioned.
wrong.C: A private meeting with the principal is not part of the challenge.
wrong.D: No certificate from teachers is described.

questions.stem: In the story, the word obligation refers to —
options: something exciting that students eagerly choose to do
something students must do, without much excitement
a prize given for reading many mystery books
a wall where students post notes about books
questions.why: The friends want reading to feel exciting rather than an obligation, something students feel they merely must do without enthusiasm.

wrong.A: An obligation is the opposite of something chosen eagerly.
wrong.C: The prize is a reward, not an obligation.
wrong.D: The book wall is an initiative, not an obligation.

questions.stem: Based on the story, why does the book wall help students who feel unsure about what to read?
options: It ranks every student by how many books they have read
It gathers real book tips from many classmates
It replaces the need for a librarian entirely
It only recommends books written by famous authors
questions.why: The wall collects short notes from classmates recommending books they truly enjoyed, giving uncertain readers quick, trustworthy suggestions.

wrong.A: The story never mentions ranking students.
wrong.C: The librarian's role is not discussed as being replaced.
wrong.D: Nothing suggests the recommendations are limited to famous authors.

questions.stem: In what order do these events happen in the story?
options: The signs are shown at the school meeting, the friends brainstorm, attendance grows
The friends brainstorm, the signs are shown at the school meeting, attendance grows
Attendance grows, the friends brainstorm, the signs are shown at the school meeting
The teacher praises the club, the friends brainstorm, attendance grows
questions.why: The friends first brainstorm their two ideas, then present signs at the school meeting, and attendance grows only afterward.

wrong.A: The brainstorming happens before the signs are made, not after.
wrong.C: Attendance cannot grow before the ideas are even introduced.
wrong.D: The teacher's praise comes at the very end, after attendance has already grown.

questions.stem: What can readers infer from the fact that students who rarely visited the library began whispering excitedly about Mystery Month?
options: The students were nervous about an upcoming test
The new initiatives sparked real curiosity and interest
The students were complaining about the library's new rules
The students disliked the signs Sara had made
questions.why: Excited whispering among previously uninterested students suggests the initiatives sparked real curiosity rather than complaints or anxiety.

wrong.A: No test is mentioned anywhere in the story.
wrong.C: No new library rules are introduced in the story.
wrong.D: The excited reaction suggests enthusiasm, not dislike of the signs.

questions.stem: Why does the author end the story by having the teacher praise the three friends during a staff meeting?
options: To emphasize how a thoughtful, creative initiative transformed a struggling club
To explain the detailed steps for organizing a staff meeting
To suggest that teachers deserve all the credit for the club's success
To describe a brand-new problem the characters must still solve
questions.why: The teacher's praise highlights the story's larger point: a small, creative initiative, built on curiosity, transformed the club's fortunes.

wrong.B: The story is not instructional about staff meetings.
wrong.C: The credit clearly belongs to Sara, Omar, and Lina's own initiative.
wrong.D: The story ends with success, not a new unresolved problem.

HIGH.prompt: The poll says a small group with a good idea can get a whole school excited about something. Do you agree or disagree? Support your argument with evidence from the story about Sara, Omar, and Lina's initiatives.
checklist: I stated a clear position on the poll statement.
I supported my position with specific evidence from the story.
I addressed at least one point someone might make against my view.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I agree that a small group with a good idea can get a whole school excited about something. In the story, only three students, Sara, Omar, and Lina, were part of the library club, yet their two initiatives, Mystery Month and the book wall, eventually made the club one of the most popular activities at the school. Someone might argue that a club needs many organizers to succeed, but this story shows that a single enthusiastic team with a genuinely creative initiative can transform how an entire student body feels about something as ordinary as reading, especially when that initiative removes the feeling of obligation and replaces it with curiosity.
